headline: Instagram's Leader Says People's Worries About AI Will Keep Growing

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: Adam Mosseri runs Instagram, an app where people share photos and videos. He talked about how many people feel upset or worried about AI, which stands for artificial intelligence. AI is technology that can create pictures, videos, or writing all by itself, without a person making it from scratch. Mosseri said he thinks people's worries about AI are going to grow even more in the next few years. Some people are artists or video makers, and they worry AI might take their jobs or copy their work without asking. Instagram now makes AI accounts put a label on themselves, kind of like a sticker that says 'this was made by a computer.' This helps people know if what they're seeing is real or made by AI. Mosseri thinks that deep down, people's biggest worry is being 'left behind,' meaning they're scared the world is changing fast and they won't be able to keep up. This matters because AI is becoming part of many apps we use every day, and people are still figuring out the best way to use it fairly.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, spoke in an interview about why so many people feel frustrated or angry about artificial intelligence (AI), which is technology that can create images, videos, and text on its own. He pointed out that some college students have even booed tech company leaders at graduation because of concerns about AI. Mosseri predicted that negative feelings toward AI will keep increasing over the next couple of years, not just among artists but among many types of workers, including engineers and mathematicians. He explained that Instagram tries not to treat AI-made content differently from regular content when deciding what to show people, but admitted the platform doesn't always rank AI posts as well. He also mentioned a problem called 'AI slop,' a phrase people use to describe low-quality AI content flooding the internet, though he thinks the term gets used too often. To help users know what's real, Instagram now requires AI-generated accounts to add a label. This is important because fake AI videos, like ones that make it look like a celebrity said something they never said, can trick people. Mosseri believes people's deepest fear isn't really about AI itself, but about being 'left behind,' meaning they're scared of losing their jobs, their creative work, or their place in a world that's changing very fast because of new technology.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: Instagram's head, Adam Mosseri, recently discussed a growing wave of negative feelings toward artificial intelligence (AI) during a podcast interview. He was responding to a question about college students booing tech executives at graduation ceremonies, a sign of how frustrated some young people feel about AI's impact. Mosseri admitted that this anger isn't limited to students or artists — it's spreading across many industries. He predicted that over the next few years, criticism and anxiety about AI will keep increasing, even if some of it isn't entirely justified. One major topic was 'AI slop,' a term people use to describe low-quality, mass-produced AI content that clutters social media feeds. Mosseri said he thinks the phrase gets overused, even though he's used it himself in the past. He also addressed how Instagram ranks content, saying the platform doesn't intentionally favor or penalize AI posts, but acknowledged that AI content often isn't ranked as effectively as content made by humans. This matters because millions of people see Instagram's recommendations every day, and how the app treats AI content affects what creators believe is worth making. Another concern is AI deepfakes — realistic fake videos or images, often of celebrities, that can mislead viewers into thinking something happened that never did. To fight this, Instagram started requiring accounts that use AI to label themselves clearly, so users can tell what's real. Still, Mosseri said banning AI content entirely isn't realistic for a platform as large as Instagram. Beyond rules and labels, Mosseri reflected on why people feel so uneasy about AI in the first place. He listed several specific fears: people worry about losing control over their own creative work, about AI systems being trained using their content without permission, about safety risks, and about losing their jobs to automation. But ultimately, he said, all these worries boil down to something simpler — a fear of being 'left behind,' meaning people are afraid technology is changing so fast that they won't be able to keep up, protect their livelihoods, or stay relevant in a changing world.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: In a recent interview on the Colin and Samir podcast, Instagram head Adam Mosseri addressed the increasingly tense relationship between the public and artificial intelligence (AI) technology. The conversation was sparked by a question about a growing trend: college students booing tech company executives during graduation speeches, a visible expression of frustration toward the industry driving AI's rapid expansion. Mosseri acknowledged that this resentment extends well beyond students or creative professionals — it's a broader cultural shift. He predicted that negativity surrounding AI will continue intensifying over the next several years, stating plainly that some of this anger will be justified while some won't be, but that it will create real challenges for people across many fields, not just the tech industry itself. A significant part of the discussion focused on content moderation. Mosseri explained that Instagram doesn't deliberately rank AI-generated posts lower than human-made ones, but he admitted that the platform likely doesn't yet rank AI content 'as well' as other content, hinting at ongoing struggles to evaluate quality fairly. He also revisited the controversial term 'AI slop,' a phrase describing low-effort, mass-produced AI content flooding social platforms. Despite having used the term himself previously, including in a year-end roundup, Mosseri now argues it's applied too broadly, potentially unfairly lumping high-quality AI work in with genuinely poor content. Another pressing issue is the spread of deceptive AI-generated media, particularly celebrity deepfakes — realistic fake videos or images designed to make it appear someone did or said something they never did. Instagram began cracking down on deceptive AI accounts in August, following the earlier introduction of labels identifying AI-generated content. Mosseri confirmed the company is still 'actively working out' how to handle these fakes, while clarifying that banning AI content outright isn't a realistic solution for a platform of Instagram's scale. Perhaps the most notable part of the interview was Mosseri's attempt to diagnose the root cause of public anxiety about AI. He listed concrete concerns: creators worried about ownership of their work, people troubled by AI systems being trained on their personal content without consent, safety concerns, and widespread fears of job displacement across professions ranging from content creation to engineering and mathematics. However, he suggested that beneath all these specific worries lies one unifying fear — the fear of being left behind as technology reshapes society faster than people can adapt.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: During an appearance on the Colin and Samir podcast focused on new video features for Instagram, company head Adam Mosseri turned to a more contentious topic: the escalating public backlash against artificial intelligence. Prompted by a question about college students booing tech executives at graduation ceremonies, Mosseri conceded that hostility toward AI is not confined to students or creative professionals — it reflects a wider societal unease. He forecast that this sentiment will only intensify in coming years, explicitly stating that the anger and anxiety, 'some of it founded, some of it unfounded,' will present difficulties for people well beyond the tech sector. This admission is notable coming from an executive at a major social platform increasingly shaped by AI tools and AI-generated content. Much of the interview dealt with how Instagram handles AI material on its platform. Mosseri maintained that Instagram does not intentionally rank AI-generated content differently from content made by humans, yet he conceded that the platform likely fails to rank AI content as effectively, raising open questions about quality control algorithms still catching up with a flood of synthetic media. He also revisited the now-common term 'AI slop,' used to describe low-quality, mass-produced AI content overwhelming feeds. Mosseri, who has previously used the phrase himself, now contends it's applied too indiscriminately, potentially discrediting legitimate or high-quality AI-assisted work alongside genuinely low-effort content. The conversation also touched on one of the more serious risks of generative AI: deceptive media, particularly celebrity deepfakes capable of convincingly fabricating speech or actions that never occurred. Instagram has taken incremental steps to address this, including introducing labels for AI-generated accounts earlier in the year and tightening enforcement against misleading AI profiles since August. Mosseri reiterated that the company is still actively determining its approach to AI fakes, while ruling out a blanket ban on AI content as impractical given Instagram's massive scale and the technology's growing ubiquity. Perhaps the most substantive portion of the interview was Mosseri's attempt to articulate the psychological roots of anti-AI sentiment. He enumerated a range of specific anxieties: creators' concerns over ownership and unauthorized use of their work to train AI models, broader safety concerns, and fears of job displacement spanning creative fields, engineering, and mathematics. Yet he argued that beneath these particular grievances lies a more fundamental anxiety — a fear of being left behind as technological change accelerates faster than individuals or institutions can adapt. This framing positions AI anxiety not merely as resistance to new tools, but as a deeper response to uncertainty about economic security, creative autonomy, and social relevance in a rapidly automating world.

questions: Have you ever felt worried about new technology changing something you care about, like a hobby, a skill, or a future job? What was that like?
Do you think social media apps should label content made by AI so people know what's real? Why might that matter to you or your friends?
Mosseri says a lot of AI worries come down to a 'fear of being left behind.' Do you agree? How do you think schools or communities could help people feel less left behind as technology changes?
